caveats.title: "same period yesterday" cannot be a strict day-ahead baseline
caveats.effect: this baseline is weaker than a true same-period-yesterday, which no forecaster could use at 11:00. Comparisons against it therefore favour the model; they are not unfair to it. It obeys the cutoff and never looks at the target day.

caveats.title: lagged baselines have no value for periods that do not exist on a clock-change day
caveats.effect: conservative and small. A clock-time match (mapping a missing period to the nearest existing one) would restore 5 nights but is a methodology change, so it has not been made.

caveats.title: the historical `forecast` field is NOT day-ahead
caveats.effect: stored as `ci_history.neso_forecast_latest_gco2_kwh`. It must NOT be used as the "NESO forecast" baseline or as a feature. The daily logger (`carbon-charge log-forecast`, table `ci_forecast_log`) records the forward 48h forecast with its issue time;

notes: These rows have no confidence intervals. Half-hours within a night are not independent, so the sample size overstates precision. For intervals on how much a forecast improves charging outcomes, use question_class='charging_value', which is scored per night.

provenance.note: All forecasts are rolling-origin backtest forecasts, as they would have been issued at 11:00 UK time on the day before the day they forecast. Nothing here is a live forecast.

content.text:
Yes, LightGBM beats `yesterday` by a wide margin, and the difference is reliable. Here's the full picture:

---

## Forecast Accuracy (MAE / RMSE, n = 30,564 half-hours)

| Model | MAE (gCO₂/kWh) | RMSE |
|---|---|---|
| **lgbm** | **19.17** | **24.70** |
| `yesterday` baseline | 43.45 | 55.95 |

LightGBM's MAE is **56% lower** than the yesterday baseline (24.3 gCO₂/kWh better). RMSE improvement is similar in magnitude.

---

## What That Means for Charging (gap_captured, n = 631 nights)

This is the more meaningful reliability test — it scores what fraction of the timer→perfect-foresight saving each strategy actually captures:

| Strategy | Gap captured | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| **lgbm** | **33.97%** | [28.4%, 38.5%] |
| `yesterday` | −21.2% | [−31.0%, −10.3%] |
| `last_week` | 1.5% | [−10.7%, +11.0%] |

The `yesterday` baseline actually performs **worse than the overnight timer** (negative gap captured) — its CI is entirely below zero, so that's reliable. LightGBM's CI is entirely above zero and far above `yesterday`'s upper bound, so the gap is real.

---

## Is the difference reliable?

**Yes, strongly.** The 95% CIs don't overlap at all:
- LightGBM lower bound: **28.4%**
- `yesterday` upper bound: **−10.3%**

There is a caveat worth noting (issue **X-2**): the `yesterday` baseline is slightly weaker than a true same-period-yesterday because of the 11:00 forecast cutoff — but this makes the comparison *more* favourable to the baseline, not less, so it doesn't inflate LightGBM's advantage.
